issue: All 8 report endpoints (network-health, inspection-compliance, regulatory-compliance, risk-register, data-quality, asset-performance, maintenance-backlog, bridge-summary) perform a full table scan on bridge.management.Bridges with no WHERE clause, then apply state filter in Node.js: `if (state) bridges = bridges.filter(b => b.state === state)`. On 5,000+ bridges this transfers all rows across the DB connection and processes them in the Node.js heap before returning a subset. Each call allocates the full bridge list in memory for every HTTP request.
fix: Add the state filter to the CDS SELECT query itself: `.where(state ? { state } : {})` inside each query builder call. This pushes the predicate to HANA/SQLite and reduces result set before network transfer. Requires touching 8 route handlers in reports-api.js.

issue: scoreAllBridges action processes each bridge in a sequential for-loop with one UPDATE or INSERT per iteration: `for (const bridge of bridges) { ... await db.run(UPDATE/INSERT) }`. For 5,000+ active bridges this serialises 5,000+ individual DB round-trips inside a single HTTP request, blocking the event loop for potentially 30-60 seconds. The action also calls computeAssetIQScore inline (pure JS) per bridge which is fine, but the DB writes are the bottleneck.
fix: Batch the upserts: build two arrays (updates[], inserts[]) during the scoring loop, then issue a single `INSERT.into().entries(inserts)` and a batch UPDATE after the loop. Reduces 5,000 round-trips to 2. Alternatively, schedule scoreAllBridges as a background job rather than a synchronous HTTP action to avoid event-loop blocking.

issue: refreshKPISnapshots fires 5-6 separate COUNT queries per state inside a sequential for-loop: `for (const state of distinctStates) { await db.run(...totals); await db.run(...overdueResult); ... }`. For 8 states + ALL = 9 iterations x 5 queries = 45 sequential DB round-trips in a single synchronous action.
fix: Issue all per-state counts in parallel: `await Promise.all(distinctStates.map(state => computeStateKPIs(state, db)))`, where computeStateKPIs issues its 5 queries via `Promise.all` internally. This collapses 45 serial round-trips to approximately 5 parallel batches.

issue: BHI/NBI virtual field computation in `after('READ', Bridges)` calls `isFeatureEnabled()` on every READ of Bridges, including list report pages. `isFeatureEnabled` issues a `SELECT.one.from('bridge.management.SystemConfig')` database query per call. Every Bridges list page load therefore incurs an additional DB query overhead that multiplies with concurrent users.
fix: Cache the feature flag result in-process with a 30-second TTL: `let _bhiCache = { val: false, ts: 0 }; async function getBhiEnabled() { if (Date.now() - _bhiCache.ts < 30000) return _bhiCache.val; _bhiCache = { val: await isFeatureEnabled('bhiBsiAssessment'), ts: Date.now() }; return _bhiCache.val; }`. Invalidate on PATCH to /system/api/features.

issue: After every READ of Bridges, the handler unconditionally runs a SELECT on AssetIQScores (`SELECT.from('bridge.management.AssetIQScores').columns('bridge_ID','ragStatus').where({bridge_ID:{in:ids}})`) regardless of whether `ragStatus` is in the OData $select clause. This adds a DB query to every Bridges list page load even when the column is not visible.
fix: Apply the same $select guard used for `activeRestrictionCount`: `const wantRag = !req.query?.$select || req.query.$select.split(',').map(f=>f.trim()).includes('ragStatus'); if (wantRag && ids.length > 0) { ... }`. Only execute the AssetIQScores JOIN when the field is requested.

issue: loadMassEditBridges() and loadMassEditRestrictions() load ALL bridge/restriction records into memory with no pagination before returning them to the Mass Edit UI. With 5,000+ bridge records this is a full table scan returned to the client in one HTTP response. The Mass Edit UI receives the complete dataset regardless of what the user intends to edit.
fix: Add server-side pagination: accept `limit` and `offset` query parameters in the /mass-edit/api/bridges endpoint; apply `.limit(limit, offset)` to the CDS SELECT query. Return `{ total, rows, limit, offset }`. The Mass Edit UI must implement client-side pagination or virtual scrolling.

issue: The in-process rate limiter (`simpleRateLimit`) uses a Node.js Map keyed by client IP. With multiple CF instances (autoscaler can scale out), each instance has its own independent Map. An attacker can distribute requests across instances to bypass the limit. The comment in code acknowledges this limitation explicitly.
fix: Replace the in-memory Map with `express-rate-limit` backed by a distributed store. Since BTP does not provide Redis natively, enforce rate limiting at the API Management gateway layer in BTP, or use a HANA-backed token bucket table with advisory lock as the shared state. At minimum, add the `X-RateLimit-Limit` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining` response headers so clients can back off gracefully.

issue: BHI/BSI computation (`computeBhiBsi`) runs entirely in the Node.js process. When the BHI feature flag is enabled and a list report returns 200+ bridges, the `after('READ', Bridges)` handler runs the computation in a for-loop for every bridge on every page load. The computation is synchronous JavaScript math — individually fast but cumulative under concurrent load.
fix: Compute BHI/NBI only when $select includes `bhi` or `nbi`, and only on detail pages (single-record requests), not list report pages. For network-wide batch scoring, use the existing `scoreAllBridges` action as the authoritative batch compute path and persist results to AssetIQScores rather than recomputing on every READ.

issue: No documented SLA exists for any BMS endpoint. The structured logger uses an ad-hoc 2000ms threshold to flag slow requests but this is not tied to any defined SLA. No p95 or p99 latency targets are documented anywhere in the project.
fix: Define endpoint SLA targets in ARCHITECTURE.md: OData list endpoints <500ms p95, Dashboard analytics <2s p95, Map clusters <1s p95, Mass upload validate <5s p95. Update the slow-request threshold in the logger to be per-endpoint. Configure BTP Alert Notification with a latency threshold alert using Application Logging correlation IDs.

issue: loadDashboardAnalytics() fetches ALL Bridges and ALL active Restrictions into Node.js memory on every dashboard page load, then computes all KPIs in-process. With 5,000+ bridges this is a large payload transferred per request with no caching. The dashboard KPIs are re-computed from scratch on every API call despite the `KPISnapshots` entity already existing for pre-computed results.
fix: Cache the dashboard analytics response in-process with a 60-second TTL (invalidated on bridge/restriction mutation). Alternatively, have the dashboard API read from the pre-computed `KPISnapshots` table (already populated by `refreshKPISnapshots`) instead of scanning the Bridges table on every request. The two approaches can coexist: serve KPISnapshots for the main dashboard tiles and use the live scan only for the detailed breakdown panels.

issue: The structured logger writes via `console.log/error/warn` rather than `@sap/logging`. Although BridgeManagement-logging (application-logs service) is bound in mta.yaml, log entries lack the structured fields required by Application Logging Service (component_id, organization_id, space_id, correlation_id as a first-class field). Correlation IDs are present in the JSON payload but not in the standard `correlation_id` header field that BTP Application Logging indexes.
fix: Install `@sap/logging` and wire it via `logging.getLogger(req.correlationId)`. Replace `console.log/warn/error` calls with `logger.info/warn/error`. This emits RFC 5424-compliant structured log entries that the Application Logging service indexes by correlation ID, enabling end-to-end trace reconstruction from the BTP Logging cockpit.

issue: Correlation ID is set on Express requests and HTTP responses but is NOT injected into the CAP CDS request context. CAP's OData handler errors are logged by CAP's internal logger without the correlation ID from the Express middleware, creating a tracing gap between Express custom routes (which have correlation IDs) and OData CAP events (which do not).
fix: After setting `req.correlationId`, propagate it into the CAP context by calling `cds.context = { http: { req, res } }` or by using `cds.middlewares` to inject the correlation ID into the CAP request object. This ensures CAP's internal error logging includes the same correlation ID as the Express access log.

issue: BridgeManagement-alert-notification service is provisioned in mta.yaml but NO alert conditions, subscriptions, or action items are configured. The service is completely inert — no error-rate alerts, no health degradation alerts, and no latency alerts will fire in production. There is no `@sap/alert-notification-client` usage anywhere in the codebase.
fix: Create an alert-notification configuration (JSON or via ANS API) defining: (1) condition on CPU/memory limit reached; (2) condition on /health endpoint returning non-200; (3) condition on 5xx error rate spike (if using Application Logging + Alert Notification integration). Subscribe these to the ops team email/PagerDuty webhook. Use `cf create-service-key BridgeManagement-alert-notification ops-key` to get API credentials for programmatic configuration.

issue: BridgeInspections and BridgeDefects CREATE/UPDATE mutations via AdminService have no audit trail entries written to ChangeLog. The recon.json confirms `hasChangeLog: false` for inspections.js and defects.js handlers. AdminService does not have `after('CREATE'/'UPDATE', BridgeInspections)` or `after('CREATE'/'UPDATE', BridgeDefects)` handlers calling `writeChangeLogs`. These are legally significant records (Civil Liability Act 2002, soft-delete only) without audit trail.
fix: Add `this.after('CREATE', BridgeInspections, ...)` and `this.after('UPDATE', BridgeInspections, ...)` handlers in admin-service.js calling `writeChangeLogs` — identical pattern to BridgeCapacities (lines 794-811 in admin-service.js). Apply the same for BridgeDefects and BridgeRiskAssessments. Verify the `before('UPDATE')` fetches the old record into `req._auditOld` before the write executes.

issue: The structured request logger uses a hardcoded 2000ms slow-request threshold for all endpoints. Map clusters, mass upload, and dashboard analytics legitimately take >2s, generating noisy 'slow: true' warnings for expected behaviour. No aggregated error-rate metric is emitted — only per-request log entries contain the status code.
fix: Define per-endpoint slow thresholds in a lookup map and select the threshold by matching `req.path`. Also emit a separate structured `{type:'metric', name:'http_error_rate', status:res.statusCode}` log entry for 4xx/5xx responses so Application Logging can aggregate error rates across the fleet.

issue: The CI pipeline has no automated deployment step. It builds and uploads the MTAR artifact but stops there — no `cf deploy` step, no automated smoke test against BTP after deployment, and no rollback trigger on failed deploy. Deployments are entirely manual. A failed deploy can go undetected if the developer does not manually run the smoke test.
fix: Add a separate `deploy` GitHub Actions job (triggered on push to main with `needs: build-and-test`) that: (1) uses `cf` CLI with a service account to deploy the built MTAR; (2) runs a smoke test: `curl -f https://<BTP-URL>/health/deep`; (3) on smoke test failure, triggers rollback via `cf deploy --abort`. Store CF_USERNAME, CF_PASSWORD, CF_ORG, CF_SPACE as GitHub Actions secrets.

issue: BridgeManagement-srv module has `health-check-type: none`. The CF router routes traffic immediately after process start, before the CAP server has finished loading the CDS model and connecting to HANA. Requests received during this startup window receive 503/connection refused errors.
fix: Change `health-check-type: none` to `health-check-type: http` with `health-check-http-endpoint: /health` and `health-check-timeout: 120`. The /health endpoint already exists and returns `{status:'UP'}`. This makes CF wait for a healthy response before registering the instance in the load balancer.

issue: No rollback procedure is documented for a failed HANA HDI schema migration. The runbook covers stuck cf deploy recovery but not the case where HDI deployer succeeds but schema migration breaks existing data. There is no documented backup/restore procedure for the HANA HDI container and no schema versioning strategy.
fix: Add a 'Schema Rollback' section to MAINTENANCE_RUNBOOK.md: (1) take a HANA HDI schema export before every deploy; (2) if HDI deploy fails post-migration, restore from export; (3) document the safe-migration pattern for additive-only changes (add nullable column, backfill, add NOT NULL in next release). Reference the `cf dmol -i <operation-id>` command for downloading full HANA deployer logs.

issue: Blue-green deployment is not configured. The mta.yaml deploys directly to the live environment with no idle slot. A deploy that fails partway through leaves the production instance in an intermediate state. The BMS serves infrastructure-critical bridge data where downtime during deploy is operationally unacceptable.
fix: Enable blue-green deploy using `cf deploy --strategy blue-green` (available in MTA deployer v1.7+, which is already the project version). This requires defining `idle-routes` on the srv module and updating the deploy command in the runbook. Test idle route behaviour with the XSUAA redirect-uri list in mta.yaml (the wildcard redirect already covers this).

issue: Three conflicting version strings exist: mta.yaml shows `version: 1.7.2`, the APP_VERSION property on the srv module is `1.0.0-nsw-standalone`, and the /health endpoint returns `process.env.npm_package_version || '1.2.0'` (hardcoded fallback). CHANGELOG.md shows 1.2.0 as the latest released version. No single source of truth for the release version exists.
fix: Designate package.json `version` as the single source of truth. Reference it in mta.yaml via a `before-all` custom build command that updates the yaml version field. Remove the hardcoded '1.2.0' fallback from /health — if `npm_package_version` is not set the health endpoint should report 'unknown' rather than a stale hardcoded string.

issue: No formal go-live checklist exists. The MAINTENANCE_RUNBOOK.md covers deployment steps but not the broader go-live gate: acceptance sign-off, data migration validation, user account provisioning, role-collection assignment verification, DNS/custom domain setup, initial KPI snapshot generation, and BAU support handover.
fix: Create `docs/GO_LIVE_CHECKLIST.md` covering pre-go-live (smoke test all 18 FLP tiles, verify role-collections, confirm HANA seed data counts, run scoreAllBridges and refreshKPISnapshots); go-live day (DNS cutover, user communication, 30-minute post-deploy monitoring); BAU handover (confirm ops team access to CF cockpit and BTP Alert Notification is active).

issue: No BAU handover package exists for the ops team. The MAINTENANCE_RUNBOOK.md is developer-oriented (CDS compile, mbt build, cf deploy commands). There is no operations guide covering: how to restart a crashed CF instance, how to check Application Logging, how to trigger the KPI refresh action from the UI, how to manage feature flags, or how to escalate to the dev team.
fix: Create `docs/BAU_OPERATIONS_GUIDE.md` covering CF cockpit instance restart, BTP cockpit HDI container health, BMS Admin workflows (Feature Flags screen, KPI Refresh, Change Documents), and escalation contacts with SLA response times. Write for a non-developer ops audience — avoid CDS/CAP jargon.

issue: No training material exists for any user role (Bridge Inspector, Bridge Manager, Operator, Viewer, Admin). The system has 8 role-collections with distinct workflows but no user guides, quick-reference cards, or onboarding walkthroughs. The Expert Council UAT feedback in CLAUDE.md noted that 30% of bridges had missing mandatory safety fields due to lack of user guidance.
fix: Create role-based quick-reference cards for the top 3 roles: (1) Bridge Inspector — create inspection, capture condition, link defects, submit for review; (2) Bridge Manager — approve condition surveys, manage permits, view risk register, export data; (3) Mass Upload Operator — step-by-step upload guide for each dataset type. Review with actual users before go-live.

issue: Complex workflows (Inspection lifecycle, Permit approval, Condition Survey Draft-Submitted-Approved, Feature Flag management) have no in-app help text, tooltips, or guided walkthroughs. Users must discover multi-step workflows by trial and error. The CLAUDE.md UAT learnings confirm this caused user confusion and data quality issues.
fix: Add `@UI.QuickInfo` annotations to all mandatory workflow fields in fiori-service.cds (already used for some fields per CLAUDE.md). Add descriptive placeholder text to free-text fields. Create a 'Getting Started' static info page in the BMS Admin shell (a UI5 view with numbered step instructions for the top 3 workflows) accessible from the left navigation.
